title: Proof: Deduction, Exhaustion, Counterexample and Contradiction
seo_title: Year 12 A Level Maths: Proof Worksheets
standard_text: Understand and use the structure of mathematical proof, proceeding from given assumptions through a series of logical steps to a conclusion; use methods of proof, including proof by deduction, proof by exhaustion and disproof by counterexample; proof by contradiction.
meta_desc: Free Year 12 A level maths worksheets on proof: proof by deduction, proof by exhaustion, disproof by counterexample, completing the square to prove inequalities and proof by contradiction. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A proof must work for every case; one counterexample disproves.
key_sub: Contradiction: assume the opposite and reach something impossible.
body_html:
How it works

Deduction: start from what you know and use algebra, e.g. n³ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1). Exhaustion: split into every possible case, e.g. n = 3k, 3k + 1, 3k + 2. Counterexample: one example that makes the statement false.

Contradiction: assume the statement is false and show this leads to something impossible. To prove √2 is irrational, assume √2 = a/b in its lowest terms.

Example

Prove x² − 6x + 10 > 0 for all real x.

x² − 6x + 10 = (x − 3)² + 1

(x − 3)² ≥ 0

Answer: It is at least 1, so always positive

Example

Disprove: n² + n + 11 is always prime.

n = 10: 100 + 10 + 11 = 121 = 11²

Answer: n = 10 is a counterexample

Common mistakes

  • Checking a few cases and calling it a proof.
  • Assuming what you want to prove in a proof by contradiction.
  • Missing a case in a proof by exhaustion.

faq.a: Splitting the problem into a finite number of cases (such as odd and even, or the remainders when dividing by 3) and proving each case.

faq.q: How does proof by contradiction work?
faq.a: Assume the statement is false, then follow logical steps to something impossible. So the statement must be true.
